THOUGHT: This 25-year-old restrained female presents with acute right groin pain and characteristic abnormal positioning of the right leg—shortened, flexed, adducted, and internally rotated—following a rear-end motor vehicle collision. This posture is highly specific for posterior hip dislocation, which commonly occurs when force is transmitted through a flexed knee (e.g., dashboard impact) driving the femoral head posteriorly out of the acetabulum. Although she was restrained, the mechanism—being the driver in a rear-end collision—can still generate sufficient anterior-directed force on the knees against the dashboard or seat, especially if her feet were braced. The associated bilateral patellar tenderness suggests concomitant knee trauma (e.g., patellar contusion or subluxation), but the dominant musculoskeletal finding is the right hip deformity. Vital signs show tachycardia (HR 116), likely due to acute pain and stress. Pelvic X-ray explicitly states “alignment suggests posterior dislocation of the right hip” despite absence of fracture—consistent with classic radiographic clues: loss of the normal teardrop sign, femoral head displaced medially and superiorly relative to the acetabulum, and/or presence of the “cymbal sign” or “inverted Y” distortion on AP pelvis. Importantly, posterior hip dislocation is an orthopedic emergency due to risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head if not reduced promptly (<6 hours optimal). Other diagnoses—such as femoral neck fracture, acetabular fracture, or lumbar radiculopathy—are less likely: no fracture seen on X-ray; neurologic exam not described but absence of reported numbness/weakness makes radiculopathy less probable; and the classic triad of shortening, flexion, adduction, and internal rotation is virtually pathognomonic for posterior hip dislocation.

DIAGNOSIS: Posterior hip dislocation
